learningObjectives.title: Anglo-Saxon England and the succession crisis
Norman control and the feudal system

questions.q: On which date did Edward the Confessor die, triggering the succession crisis of 1066?
questions.explain: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 without a clear, undisputed heir.

questions.q: Who was crowned King of England on 6 January 1066, the day after Edward's death?
questions.explain: Harold Godwinson was crowned almost immediately, claiming Edward had named him on his deathbed.

questions.q: What was the name of the Anglo-Saxon council of leading nobles that advised the king and endorsed his successor?
questions.explain: The Witan was the assembly of powerful nobles and churchmen that advised the king and confirmed Harold's succession.

questions.q: On what basis did William of Normandy justify his claim to the English throne?
options: Edward had promised him the throne and Harold had sworn an oath to support him
He was Edward's eldest son and legal heir
He had been elected by the Witan in 1065
He was the reigning King of Norway with a Viking claim
questions.explain: William argued Edward had named him heir and that Harold had sworn a sacred oath to help him become king.

questions.q: Which rival claimant to the throne in 1066 was the King of Norway?
questions.explain: Harald Hardrada, King of Norway, invaded northern England pressing a Viking claim to the throne.

questions.q: Why was the House of Godwin so powerful in England by 1066?
options: They controlled the most important earldoms and were the wealthiest family after the king
They were the direct royal bloodline descended from Alfred the Great
They had been appointed by the Pope to rule England
They commanded the only professional army in the country
questions.explain: The Godwins held several major earldoms, giving them land, wealth and influence second only to the king.

questions.q: Why did the Northumbrians rebel against Earl Tostig Godwinson in 1065?
options: They resented his harsh rule and heavy taxation
He had converted the region to Norman customs
He refused to defend them against the Scots
He had sworn loyalty to William of Normandy
questions.explain: Tostig's severe government and high taxes provoked a Northumbrian revolt that led to his exile.

questions.q: Edgar Aethling had the strongest hereditary blood claim in 1066 but was passed over as king. What best explains this?
options: He was a young boy with no military experience or powerful supporters
He had already been promised to William of Normandy
He was excluded because he was not of royal descent
He had been captured by Harald Hardrada
questions.explain: Despite his royal blood, Edgar was too young and lacked the powerful backing needed in a time of crisis.

questions.q: At which battle on 25 September 1066 did Harold Godwinson defeat and kill Harald Hardrada?
questions.explain: Harold destroyed the Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, where both Hardrada and Tostig were killed.

questions.q: On what date was the Battle of Hastings fought?
questions.explain: William defeated Harold at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066.

questions.q: Why was Harold's army at a disadvantage at the Battle of Hastings?
options: They were exhausted after marching south from the battle at Stamford Bridge
They had no experienced soldiers or housecarls
They were greatly outnumbered by the Norman infantry
They had run out of weapons and armour
questions.explain: Harold's men were tired and depleted after fighting at Stamford Bridge and marching rapidly to the south coast.

questions.q: How did the Norman tactic of the 'feigned retreat' help William win at Hastings?
options: It lured English soldiers out of the shield wall so they could be cut down
It allowed the Normans to escape and regroup at their ships
It gave archers time to reload their crossbows
It tricked Harold into surrendering early
questions.explain: By pretending to flee, the Normans tempted the English to break their shield wall and pursue, exposing them to cavalry.

questions.q: William wanted a detailed record of who held which land and how much it was worth so he could assess taxes and resources. What did he commission in 1086 to achieve this?
questions.explain: The Domesday Book was a comprehensive land survey used to record ownership, value and tax liability.

questions.q: Which combination of Norman strengths most directly broke the English shield wall at Hastings?
options: Cavalry charges combined with feigned retreats
Massed longbow volleys and pike squares
questions.explain: Mounted knights and feigned retreats drew the English off the ridge and broke their previously solid shield wall.

questions.q: What type of castle did the Normans build quickly across England to secure control after 1066?
questions.explain: Motte and bailey castles could be raised quickly from earth and timber to dominate an area.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of the castles the Normans built across England?
options: To dominate and control the local population and act as a military base
To provide homes for Anglo-Saxon earls
To store the harvest and collect church tithes
To serve mainly as places of worship
questions.explain: Castles intimidated the population and gave Norman troops a secure base from which to control the surrounding area.

questions.q: Why did William order the Harrying of the North in 1069-70?
options: To permanently crush northern resistance by devastating the region
To reward loyal Anglo-Saxon earls with new land
To convert the north to the Norman Church
To prepare the north for a Viking alliance
questions.explain: William destroyed villages, crops and livestock across the north to end repeated rebellions there for good.

questions.q: A Norman tenant-in-chief refuses to supply the knights he owes when the king demands them. Under the feudal system, what is the king entitled to do?
options: Double the size of the baron's estates
Make the baron a housecarl in the royal guard
Send the baron on a pilgrimage to Rome
questions.explain: Land was held in return for service, so failing to provide knights could lead to the land being forfeited to the king.

questions.q: In the Norman feudal system, what did tenants-in-chief owe the king in return for holding their land?
options: Paying a share of the harvest to the Church
Building a cathedral on their estate
questions.explain: Tenants-in-chief held land from the king in exchange for supplying a set number of knights for military service.

questions.q: Whom did William make Archbishop of Canterbury in 1070, replacing the Anglo-Saxon Stigand?
questions.explain: William appointed Lanfranc as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1070 to reform and control the English Church.
